content: The tubing connected to venous and arterial catheters can contribute to bloodstream infections, including bacteraemia. The frequency of replacing these administration sets may influence the risk of such infections. This review, initially published in 2005 and updated in 2012, aimed to determine whether the timing of administration set replacement affects rates of microbial colonization, infection, and mortality. To conduct this review, researchers searched multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, CINAHL, and EMBASE, covering studies up to June 2012. They also reviewed reference lists of identified trials and contacted experts in the field. No language restrictions were applied. The review included randomized or controlled clinical trials that examined the frequency of administration set replacement in hospitalized patients with venous or arterial catheters. Two reviewers independently assessed the studies for inclusion, resolving disagreements through discussion with a third reviewer. Data were collected on seven outcomes: catheter-related infection, infusate-related infection, microbial colonization of the catheter or infusate, all-cause bloodstream infection, mortality, and cost. Results from studies comparing different replacement intervals (e.g., every 96 hours versus every 72 hours, or every 48 hours versus every 24 hours) were pooled for analysis. The updated review included 16 studies involving 5001 participants, with study populations ranging from neonates to adults. These studies examined various administration sets, including those used for parenteral nutrition, lipid emulsions, and crystalloid infusions. Most studies had a moderate to high risk of bias or lacked sufficient detail on methods to minimize bias. Due to the nature of the intervention, blinding of personnel was not possible in any of the included trials. The analysis found no significant differences in the rates of catheter-related or infusate-related bacteraemia or fungaemia when comparing more frequent versus less frequent administration set replacement. The risk ratios (RR) for these outcomes were 1.06 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.67 to 1.69) and 0.67 (95% CI 0.27 to 1.70), respectively. However, less frequent replacement of administration sets was associated with a reduced rate of bloodstream infections (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.98). There was no evidence of differences in catheter or infusate colonization with more frequent replacement (RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.24; RR 1.15, 95% CI 0.70 to 1.86, respectively). In the neonatal population, there was borderline evidence suggesting that infrequent administration set replacement might increase mortality (RR 1.84, 95% CI 1.00 to 3.36). No significant interactions were found between the frequency of administration set replacement and subgroups such as parenteral nutrition versus non-parenteral nutrition infusates, adult versus neonatal participants, or arterial versus venous catheters. The authors concluded that administration sets not containing lipids, blood, or blood products can be safely left in place for up to 96 hours without increasing the risk of infection. However, there is some evidence suggesting that infrequent replacement may increase mortality in neonates. It is important to note that much of the evidence was derived from studies of low to moderate quality, which limits the strength of these conclusions.
